title: Greatest common divisor: trial divisors vs Euclid's algorithm
problem_statement: Given non-negative integers a and b, compute gcd(a, b), the largest integer dividing both (with gcd(a, 0) = a and gcd(0, 0) = 0).

input.parameter: n = bit length of max(a, b); both inputs are < 2^n.
input.size_measure: 2n bits at most (standard binary encoding of a and b).

algorithms.name: trial divisors
algorithms.idea: Try d = min(a, b), min(a, b) - 1, ... and return the first d that divides both a and b.
algorithms.pseudocode: if a = 0 or b = 0: return a + b; d = min(a, b); while d does not divide both a and b: d = d - 1; return d
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(2^n) iterations in the worst case: for a, b >= 1 exactly min(a, b) - gcd(a, b) + 1 iterations of one or two divisions (none if a = 0 or b = 0); for n >= 2 the maximum over inputs with max(a, b) of bit length n is 2^n - 2, attained by the coprime pair (2^n - 1, 2^n - 2); the coprime Fibonacci pairs used for V2 need F_k >= 2^n / 3 > 2^(n-2) iterations (the pair is F_(k+1), F_k with F_(k+1) < 2^n <= F_(k+2), and F_(k+2) = F_(k+1) + F_k <= 3 F_k). In bit operations: at most 2^n iterations with at most two divisions of numbers below 2^n each, i.e. O(2^n n^2) with schoolbook division.
algorithms.correctness: Every common divisor is at most min(a, b) (for a, b > 0), and d = 1 always divides both, so the first d found scanning downwards is the greatest common divisor.

algorithms.name: Euclid's algorithm
algorithms.idea: Replace (a, b) by (b, a mod b) until b = 0; the common divisors never change.
algorithms.pseudocode: while b != 0: (a, b) = (b, a mod b); return a
algorithms.time_complexity: O(n) division steps: at most log_phi(min(a, b)) + 2 < 1.4405 n + 2 if min(a, b) >= 1, and at most one step otherwise (after Lamé 1844; PROOFS.md section 5). Consecutive Fibonacci numbers are the worst case: the smallest pair a > b >= 1 that needs k steps is (F_(k+2), F_(k+1)), and the V2 pair (F_(k+1), F_k) needs k - 1 = 1.44 n + O(1) steps for n >= 2. O(n^2) bit operations with schoolbook division: a step with quotient q on numbers below 2^n costs O(n (1 + log2 max(q, 1))), and the quotients q >= 1 multiply to at most max(a, b) < 2^n; Theta(n^2) on the Fibonacci pairs, where the step dividing F_(j+1) by F_j reads at least (j - 1) log2(phi) bits.
algorithms.correctness: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b) because a mod b = a - qb, so both pairs have the same common divisors; the second argument strictly decreases, and gcd(a, 0) = a.

relationship: Trial divisors are linear in the VALUE min(a, b), hence exponential, Theta(2^n), in the bit length n. Euclid needs only O(n) division steps (after Lamé 1844) and O(n^2) bit operations: polynomial in the input size.

sources.title: The Art of Computer Programming, Vol. 2: Seminumerical Algorithms (3rd ed.)
Note sur la limite du nombre des divisions dans la recherche du plus grand commun diviseur entre deux nombres entiers
sources.venue: Comptes Rendus de l'Académie des Sciences (Paris)

verification.method: V1: both implementations agree with each other and with math.gcd (used only as the oracle) on random pairs with max(a, b) of bit length n = 0..16, 32, 64, 256, 1024 and 4096 (trial divisors up to n = 16), including pairs with a large common factor and pairs with a zero. V2 uses consecutive Fibonacci numbers, the largest pair below 2^n: they are coprime (worst case for trial divisors) and the worst case for Euclid (PROOFS.md, section 5). Trial divisors fit 2^n at n = 14..22. Euclid is timed at n = 4000..64000 bits against n^2; the fit is a measurement on these Fibonacci pairs, not a check of the O(n^2) bit-operation bound (the cost of a division step on CPython's multi-digit integers is not analysed here). The O(n) step count itself is not timed: at word size (n <= 64) wall-clock time is dominated by interpreter overhead and CPython's 30-bit digit boundaries (a trial fit against n gave alpha ~1.34), so it does not isolate the step count. Instead it is proved in PROOFS.md and counted exactly by tests/test_proofs_gcd.py. Proofs: PROOFS.md proves every claim of this entry (correctness, iteration and step counts, bit-operation and space bounds) and names the deterministic tests that check each one.

caveats: Bit-size view: trial divisors are polynomial (linear) in the VALUE of the inputs and exponential only in their length. Euclid's O(n^2) bit cost assumes schoolbook division; faster gcd algorithms are background (cited, not claimed). V2 times Euclid on numbers with thousands of bits; that fit is a measurement on Fibonacci pairs, not a check of the O(n^2) bit-operation bound. The O(n) division-step bound is not timed; it is proved in PROOFS.md and the steps are counted exactly by tests/test_proofs_gcd.py.
notes: History and faster gcd algorithms: see background. PROOFS.md section 5 also proves a decimal form of the step bound (at most 5 steps per decimal digit of b, for a >= b >= 1).

background.statement: Faster (subquadratic) gcd algorithms, based on the half-gcd method, exist.
Euclid's algorithm goes back to Euclid's Elements.
Lamé (1844) bounded the number of division steps of Euclid's algorithm.
